articles.title: Problems brewing for the proper pint as Camra membership falls
articles.summary: Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinationals are threatening to squeeze out independent breweries. For centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer.
body: Real ale is a traditional draught cask beer, a “living” product that is produced and stored in its cask. It differs from a cold, fizzy lager, in which the yeast is killed and carbon dioxide is added. Real ale contains live yeast so it continues fermenting until it is served.

Outside the Devonshire pub in Soho, central London, there is an ever-present horde of drinkers downing pints of Guinness, a stout made by the multinational company Diageo. But the landlord and co-owner Oisín Rogers says: “Real ale is all I drink.”

He says: “It is a properly handmade British product produced in exactly the same way it has been for centuries. It has never been industrialised like some of the other drinks that are for sale in bars in London.” His favourite tipple, is, appropriately, a pint of Landlord, made by the family-owned Timothy Taylor brewery in Keighley, West Yorkshire.

Tom Stainer, Camra’s chief executive, says independent breweries are facing unfair competition from multinationals. If you walk into a pub on the high street, you are often confronted with the same few beers, most of which are made by the same large companies, Stainer says.

For centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer.

articles.title: ‘Standard’ velvet hangers? There’s nothing standard about some of the items on John Lewis’s uni essentials list| Emma Beddington
articles.summary: It used to be that dorm rooms were chaotically messy. Does this new generation really need an £80 spice rack and velvet clothes hangers? Of all the questions this year’s freshers may be nervously asking themselves as they prepare for this next phase – did I pick the right course?
body: Fret no longer, enquiring young minds: John Lewis has the answer on its packing checklist for students. Thirty to 40, it claims, wildly, “consisting mostly of standard velvet or plastic hangers”. “Standard” velvet? I missed this memo.

I found the list via the student news site the Tab, which posted a TikTok mocking J-Lew’s notions of what constitute “essentials”: a £495 Marc Jacobs bag, a £399 desk and an £80 spice rack carousel (I also spotted a £185 Ralph Lauren quarter-zip for those must-attend “man in finance” costume parties).

In fairness, most of the stuff on there is fine, but the Stanley cups and shower squeegees conjure a slightly dispiriting picture of wellness-focused, sensible, hygienic youth. I know that’s their generation’s reputation, but it would be nice if parents could be persuaded not to stock up, instead letting them go rogue and fill their kitchens, bathrooms and bedrooms with chaotically impractical stuff they choose themselves. Isn’t that what early adulthood is all about?

Does this new generation really need an £80 spice rack and velvet clothes hangers?

articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Ernie the danger dog – who loves dicing with death
articles.summary: He has chased a deer across a dual carriageway, eaten an entire tray of chocolate brownies and jumped head first into a canal. But despite all the worry he brings us, he is extraordinarily lovable.
body: Ernie found his way into our hearts and home about nine years ago, when he strategically crawled into my lap during a family visit to meet a litter of puppies. While all the other beagle puppies ran wild, Ernie sat comfortably on me with his long, soft ears dangling down. We chose him because of his placid nature and named him Ernie after my mum’s late dad, who coincidentally also had short legs and a bit of a round belly.
After a few weeks we realised that Ernie was anything but placid. His gentle temperament quickly morphed into an unruly and persistent need to find his way into danger.

The most shocking incident happened one morning in November 2022. Ernie spotted a deer in the forest behind our house. He darted away from me and my mum, through the forest and towards a busy dual carriageway. Ignoring our screams, Ernie crossed the road, missing multiple lorries and cars, making his way to safety on a small patch of grass on the pavement. It was a miracle he had managed to avoid injury.
points: He has chased a deer across a dual carriageway, eaten an entire tray of chocolate brownies and jumped head first into a canal.
But despite all the worry he brings us, he is extraordinarily lovable.

articles.title: In Japan's Niigata Prefecture, the Ancient Culinary Tradition of Fermentation Is Very Much Alive
articles.summary: From prized sake to pickled potato salad and snow-aged ham, here's how to sip and savor your way through a part of the country known for its fermented foods.
body: My first stop was Willow House, a café and bakery where washi lanterns cast gentle light onto the natural-wood interiors and jazz seeps from the speakers. It's part of the Suzu Group, a coterie of restaurants, izakayas, and guesthouses that have put a modern spin on Niigata's ancient culinary craft. The bakery churns out a rotation of sourdough breads, caramelized apple rolls, and gratin toast with dashi-infused béchamel, while the café has a snack menu featuring miso pickled potato salad, fermented summer tomato salsa, and snow-aged ham.

I continued the tour with a skewer of rice dumplings coated in a sticky-sweet fermented soy sauce glaze at the takeaway counter of Eguchi Dango, a historic fourth-generation wagashi sweets shop. Next is a visit to the Settaya 6th Avenue Fermentation Museum Komegura, located in the former warehouse of a “saffron sake” brewery. Its exterior is decorated with colorful Chinese zodiac panels, while inside is a lab with exhibits on fermentation and a café. Its gift shop sells miso; amazake, a nutritious rice-and-koji drink known for its alleged longevity benefits; and bottles of saffron liqueur made from a recipe that was patented in 1884.
points: From prized sake to pickled potato salad and snow-aged ham, here's how to sip and savor your way through a part of the country known for its fermented foods.

articles.title: 7 Stylish Ways to Wear a Barn Jacket This Fall
articles.summary: A Fashion Week mainstay—from New York to Copenhagen—the barn jacket is a beloved transitional staple. Here are 7 ways to wear it, plus the best styles to shop.
body: Championed on the runways at Prada, Toteme, and The Row—and spotted at nearly every fashion week, from New York to Copenhagen—the barn jacket remains the ultimate transitional staple. While men’s barn jackets originated in the ’20s as utilitarian workwear, they’ve since been adopted for everyday use, becoming a fixture in the wardrobes of everyone from the British royal family to Gigi Hadid and Zoë Kravitz.

The jacket’s signature design details—a boxy silhouette, multiple pockets, button or snap closures, leather or corduroy collar, and durable, often waxed fabric—make it perfectly practical, but also give it that distinct no-fuss, unpretentious appeal. Its simplicity and versatility are akin to that of a great pair of blue jeans.

articles.title: Is Sleeping Under Canvas the Secret to Better Rest?
articles.summary: Here’s why traveling to sleep in a tent could improve your sleep patterns long after you check out—plus, five of the best places in the world to do it.
body: For something so fundamental, sleep has become surprisingly complicated. We track it, optimize it, travel in search of it—fueling a fast-growing sleep tourism industry built on blackout blinds, circadian lighting, and AI-calibrated mattresses. And yet, for all this innovation, the most effective reset often lies in something far simpler: stepping outside, and more specifically, sleeping under canvas.

I’ve felt it myself, in ways no hotel room, however luxurious, has ever quite managed to replicate. From bedding down to the lullabies of the bush in fly camps across wild corners of Africa, to a WiFi-free ranch in Wyoming with a what-dreams-are-made-of glamping meadow: the steady rush of a snow-melt creek just beyond my tent, a constant thread of white noise that softened everything around it. After days spent entirely outdoors, moving my body, with almost zero screen time—whether on safari or in the saddle, moving through vast landscapes, syncing to the sunset and the stars—the effect was the same. I slept more deeply, woke more easily, and felt, for once, properly rested.

articles.title: Chang-rae Lee's Guide to Umbria
articles.summary: In late 2019, the author—whose new novel is out this month—and his wife purchased a modest former farm property in northern Umbria. Here, he reveals highlights of the region.
body: While he has yet to write about the region, he finished his two novels in the old stone house “that’s always cool even in the high summer heat,” including this month’s A Tender Age (Riverhead), about a child of Korean immigrants navigating adolescence.

“Although we don’t venture out every day, over the years we’ve explored much of this area of the Upper Tiber River Valley, the Alto Tevere,” he says. Here, wisdom he’s gained as a result of that exploration.

Restaurants: Our houseguests always ask this first, because of course eating well is a primary objective when here. Because black summer truffles are usually abundant in Umbria, I steer folks to two truffle-centric eateries, Da Baffone, which is perched far up in the hills above the medieval town of Gubbio, and the more easily accessed Osteria del Boccajolo in Umbertide. Both places will shock you with the abundance of truffle shavings that practically covers the handmade tagliatelle, or the scrambled eggs, and even the steak. Amazing stuff.
